title: Temperature-Color Interaction: Subjective Indoor Environmental Perception and Physiological Responses in Virtual Reality
research_question: Temperature-color interaction effects on subjective perception and physiological responses are investigated using a novel hybrid experimental method combining thermal and visual stimuli from real and virtual reality (VR) environments, respectively.

participants.description: Initially 72 participants (36 men, 36 women), 15 excluded due to technical problems, resulting in 57 (27 at 24°C, 30 at 29°C). Age range 18–32 years, normal BMI, full color vision, no drugs/alcohol, generally healthy, C1 English proficiency. Participants were from Switzerland.
participants.recruitment: Not explicitly stated, but selected based on eligibility criteria.

stimuli_or_exposures.description: Three colored daylight conditions (blue, orange, neutral) simulated in VR using HDR images of a mock office setting, representing daylight entering through fully transparent colored filters (visible transmittance 37%-40%). Chromatic coordinates provided (Table 2).
stimuli_or_exposures.source: Method, Stimuli section, Figure 1, Table 2, Figure 2

stimuli_or_exposures.description: Two temperature levels (24°C and 29°C) controlled by a radiant system in a test room. Relative humidity 45%-55%, air velocity < 0.1 m/s. Measured temperatures were 23.9°C (SD 0.8) for 24°C neutral, 23.7°C (SD 0.5) for 24°C blue, 23.9°C (SD 0.6) for 24°C orange; 29.0°C (SD 1.6) for 29°C neutral, 29.7°C (SD 1.4) for 29°C blue, 29.0°C (SD 1.2) for 29°C orange.
stimuli_or_exposures.source: Method, Stimuli section, Equipment section, Table 4

measures.instrument: iButtons data loggers (DS1921H-F5) at neck, right scapula, right shin, left hand

mechanisms: Cross-modal effect of color on thermal perception (hue-heat hypothesis): colors toward red perceived as warm, blue as cool.
SCL/nSCR changes related to arousal and attention level rather than thermal stress.
Thermal factor prevails over visual factor in uncomfortable thermal environments for overall evaluation.
Short exposure time to thermal environment might not allow for full thermal adaptation.
VR visual stimulus might be more predominant, masking temperature effects on color evaluation.
moderators: AT (difference between experimental and measured temperature)
implementation_implications: Glazing with orange color shift should be used with caution in slightly warm environments due to perceived warmer thermal perception and lower acceptability.
Findings can be applied to the design of buildings using new glazing technologies with saturated colors, such as transparent photovoltaics.

The hybrid VR experimental method is a promising instrument for future studies on indoor factor interactions, especially when visual stimuli need to be controlled and precise timestamps for physiological responses are needed.

limitations: Limited sample size for between-subject analyses.
Short exposure time to thermal and visual stimuli, potentially limiting full adaptation.
VR use might have directed more attention to visual conditions, masking temperature effects on color evaluation.
Lack of complete-body immersion in VR (e.g., not showing hands).
Bare look of the space and lack of variations in indoor objects and furniture, potentially affecting visual judgment and temperature effects.
Use of saturated colors in glazing, less common than less saturated ones.
Color-scheme of external view might influence color evaluation more than daylight color itself.

paper_metadata.crossref_title: Temperature–Color Interaction: Subjective Indoor Environmental Perception and Physiological Responses in Virtual Reality
paper_metadata.crossref_journal: Human Factors: The Journal of the Human Factors and Ergonomics Society
paper_metadata.crossref_abstract: Objective Temperature–color interaction effects on subjective perception and physiological responses are investigated using a novel hybrid experimental method combining thermal and visual stimuli from real and virtual reality (VR) environments, respectively. Background Despite potential building design applications, studies combining temperature with daylight transmitted through colored glazing are limited due to hard-to-control light conditions. VR is identified as a promising experimental tool for such investigations that overcomes the limitations of experiments using daylight. Method Fifty-seven people participated in an experiment combining three colored glazing (orange/blue/neutral) and two temperatures (24°C/29°C). Exposed to one color–temperature combination, participants evaluated their thermal, visual, and overall perception, whereas their physiological responses (heart rate, skin conductance, and skin temperature) were continuously measured. Results Daylight color significantly affected thermal perception, whereas no significant effects of temperature on visual perception were found. Acceptability of the workspace was affected by both color and temperature. Cross-modal effects from either daylight color or temperature levels on physiological responses were not observed. Conclusion In the VR setting, the orange daylight led to warmer thermal perception in (close-to-) comfortable temperatures, resulting in a color-induced thermal perception and indicating that orange glazing should be used with caution in a slightly warm environment. Application Findings can be applied to the design of buildings using new glazing technologies with saturated colors, such as transparent photovoltaics. Despite some limitations, the hybrid environment is suggested as a promising experimental tool for future studies on indoor factor interactions.
